/world/2026/oct/30/canada-european-union.headline: EU leaders to press Burnham to pay more towards Ukraine’s defence
/world/2026/oct/30/canada-european-union.excerpt: EU leaders will press Andy Burnham at a summit in Brussels to contribute more to Ukraine’s defence effort in 2027. EU officials argue that the UK, Canada and Japan should do more to support Ukraine, but entreaties to these G7 countries for extra financial aid at recent international meetings have not been answered, Brussels says. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, will call on the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, to contribute to Ukraine’s looming financial shortfall at an EU-Canada summit in Montreal next week. A similar request to the British prime minister will be made when he meets von der Leyen and the European Council president, António Costa, for a long-awaited EU-UK summit on 20 November in Brussels. It comes as the UK chancellor, John Healey, prepares for his first budget next week, weighing numerous calls for more spending against the rising cost of government borrowing and a darkening economic outlook. Healey said earlier this month he was “working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine – military, diplomatic and economic”. Ukraine says it faces a €70bn (£58bn) funding shortfall in 2027 to pay for its defence and civilian needs. The EU and its member states are paying for 80% of Ukraine’s financial needs, according to the commission, which considers a “fair” EU share to be two-thirds, with the remaining third covered by other allies.
/world/2026/oct/30/canada-european-union.trail: Officials will call on UK to ‘step up’ financial support at Brussels summit – with post-Brexit issues also on agenda

/world/2026/oct/30/canada-european-union.headline: EU drops sponsorship of disinformation conference at Trump officials’ request
/world/2026/oct/30/canada-european-union.excerpt: The Trump administration pressured multiple countries to withdraw their sponsorship of a leading European conference on disinformation, with Canada, Lithuania and the EU’s diplomatic service subsequently agreeing to do so, the Guardian understands. The conference, #Disinfo2026, taking place on Wednesday and Thursday, is the annual meetup of Europe’s counter-disinformation community and has drawn hundreds of researchers, journalists, technologists and policymakers to a hotel in Vilnius, Lithuania. It is run by an independent Brussels non-profit, EU Disinfo Lab. Days before the conference, the logos of its main supporters – the Lithuanian ministry of foreign affairs, the European External Action Service (EEAS) and Global Affairs Canada, the country’s foreign ministry – were wiped off its website. Photos of the event shared with the Guardian also show white stickers affixed over the logos of these organisations printed on official conference materials, appearing to indicate they were struck from the program in haste. Three persons familiar with the matter, including European officials, confirmed that the US state department had been in touch with multiple governments over their support for the conference. Internal state department documents seen by the Guardian also show US officials thanking Lithuania for “taking US concerns seriously”.
/world/2026/oct/30/canada-european-union.trail: Lithuania and Canada were also pressured to withdraw, and days before #Disinfo2026, logos were wiped off website

/world/2026/oct/30/canada-european-union.headline: A new leaf: inside the 25 September Guardian Weekly
/world/2026/oct/30/canada-european-union.excerpt: The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, last week extended an unprecedented offer to Canada, inviting it to become the EU’s first “associate member”. For our big story this week, Brussels correspondent Jennifer Rankin explores what the proposed alliance might mean. While there is a lot of common ground for the two parties, she writes, their agreement raises many questions and is clouded in uncertainty. Meanwhile, senior correspondent Lisa O’Carroll examines the possible implications for the UK – asking whether it offers a blueprint for Britain, or a reminder it is out in the cold. Then, former White House speechwriter Ted Widmer says Canadian prime minister Mark Carney’s remarks before the European parliament set out what a new west might look like, without its most powerful member – the US. /world/2026/oct/30/canada-european-union.headline: The EU’s Canada offer is more mood than reality but it could hint at a future geometry for the bloc
/world/2026/oct/30/canada-european-union.excerpt: The EU and Canada, Ursula von der Leyen said last week, “see the world with the same eyes”, with shared stances on everything from AI to the climate crisis, the Ukraine war and the unholy chaos unleashed by the current occupant of the White House (OK, she didn’t actually say that last bit. But I like to think she almost certainly thought it.) So, the European Commission president went on, Canada should become “the first associate member of the EU”. In the audience, Mark Carney beamed with delight. The next day, Canada’s prime minister enthusiastically embraced the idea of an “alliance for the future”, to build “collective resilience” through “deep cooperation”. Cue standing ovations, warm handshakes – and a great deal of head-scratching in Brussels and assorted EU capitals. Because “associate membership” of the EU is not, in fact, a thing. Nor, as a Guardian editorial pointed out, is there “any blueprint for what such a thing might involve”. The term was, the editorial argued, “a political hypothesis”, describing “a relationship of intimate strategic alignment with the EU, stopping short of actual membership, in ways that are significant but undefined”. So what exactly are the commission and Canada playing at here, and where might it lead? You can see where they’re coming from. On paper, in a world of unpredictable and increasingly aggressive great powers, it makes perfect sense.
/world/2026/oct/30/canada-european-union.trail: While Brussels and Ottawa desire a deeper partnership born of Trump-era volatility, ​the EU has no legal framework to accommodate it

/world/2026/oct/30/canada-european-union.headline: Canada’s Carney embraces EU associate membership proposal
/world/2026/oct/30/canada-european-union.excerpt: Mark Carney has welcomed the goal of Canada becoming the EU’s first associate member, calling for “deep cooperation” between Europe and his country to secure their sovereignty, after Donald Trump derided the idea as “laughable”. In an address to the European parliament in Strasbourg, the Canadian prime minister said polling showed that an overwhelming majority of Canadians supported much closer ties with Europe. “Canada welcomes this idea,” he said, referring to European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s pitch that Canada should become the EU’s first associate member. “Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities,” Carney said on Thursday, listing sectors including critical minerals, energy security and AI. Von der Leyen had on Wednesday invited Canada to become the EU’s first associate member in a speech in which she declared she wanted to bring the bilateral relationship “to the highest level possible”. A few hours later, Trump threatened “very serious tariffs” on Europe if the plan went ahead. Asked about Trump’s threats, Carney told reporters: “Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak.

/football/2026/oct/30/ballon-dor-betting.headline: Alexia Putellas a worthy Ballon d’Or winner but the limited shortlist illustrates flaws
/football/2026/oct/30/ballon-dor-betting.excerpt: After a four-year wait, Alexia Putellas is the queen of women’s football once again. Receiving the Ballon d’Or for a record‑equalling third time to continue Spain’s domination of the award, the 32-year-old reinforces her status as one of the greatest players of all time. It was the sixth consecutive year in which the honour went to either Putellas or her international teammate Aitana Bonmatí, and it was symbolic of Putellas’s resurgence after her comeback from the anterior cruciate ligament injury she sustained in 2022, her refusal to surrender her career to that setback, and her majestic rise back to the top. The midfielder’s competition‑leading 14 goal contributions – eight goals and six assists – in 11 Women’s Champions League appearances last season, helping Barcelona to lift the trophy, went a long way to her securing the most votes, as well as her starring role in Spain’s victory in the Nations League finals last December. Her new club, London City Lionesses, will rejoice in the prestige of having the Ballon d’Or winner in their squad but Putellas, who spent 14 years at Barcelona, made it clear whom she wanted to thank.
/football/2026/oct/30/ballon-dor-betting.trail: Neglect of African football and a third win for the Spanish great does little to challenge narrative that the prize is reserved only for players of the top nations

/football/2026/oct/30/ballon-dor-betting.headline: Team success, the ‘Bundesliga tax’ and the World Cup: three takeaways from the 2026 Ballon d’Or
/football/2026/oct/30/ballon-dor-betting.excerpt: It was an awards show that, as Michael Owen admitted, could have been a phone call – as it was in 2001 when he won. A quarter-century on, a ballroom full of footballers, power brokers, a gravity-defying dancer and a handful of heckling rabble-rousers plodded through a three-hour slog of a ceremony. Aside from a reminder to viewers at home just how precious our free time is, what could be gleaned from the men’s element of the Ballon d’Or ceremony? It’s hard to stand out in a team game As early voting for the midterms progresses in the United States, the party affiliation of a candidate carries as much weight as their name. This year, as with many this century, the panel of voters were similarly interested in team performance beyond individual accomplishments. Not to say that Harry Kane didn’t make a strong individual case to win. The presumptive frontrunner this year, Kane also took home the honor as top men’s striker of the year roughly 45 minutes before the top prize went his way. Scoring 64 goals in 56 club matches is staggering. So, too, is his growing reputation as a world-class chance creator with the through balls he threads with increasing ease. Kane stands out as a stat-accumulator in a waning era of meticulous systems, and his gilded peers playing for teams operating off such intricate models were largely held back. Premier League-winning Arsenal also reached the Champions League final, yet none of their players ranked higher than 15th (Declan Rice).

/football/2026/oct/30/ballon-dor-betting.headline: Harry Kane claims men’s Ballon d’Or to end England’s 25-year wait for winner
/football/2026/oct/30/ballon-dor-betting.excerpt: Harry Kane is the Ballon d’Or winner for 2026, the first Englishman to win football’s most prestigious individual trophy in 25 years. Two hours into a lavishly excitable ceremony at the Palladium Theatre in London, Kane’s name emerged from the final envelope to wild cheers inside the auditorium. The women’s Ballon d’Or, awarded moments earlier, was won by Alexia Putellas of London City Lionesses, a third Ballon, five years on from her first in the colours of Barcelona. In the men’s voting, Kane finished ahead of co-favourites Lamine Yamal of Barcelona and Kylian Mbappé of Real Madrid, an outcome that will perhaps cause the familiar consternation among the hierarchy of those clubs, not to mention the vast online fan army attached to the superstar players in Kane’s wake. But Kane is also a fully deserving winner of football’s ultimate gong. The trophy, organised by magazine France Football (owned by L’Équipe Group), is awarded by a vote of journalists and administrators across the footballing super-scape. For Kane, it is reward for a year during which he has won the European Golden Boot, played a major role in Bayern Munich’s Bundesliga title, captained England to a World Cup semi-final, and above all shown himself to be a wonderfully humble superstar player.
/football/2026/oct/30/ballon-dor-betting.trail: Harry Kane became first Englishman in 25 years to win men’s Ballon d’Or with Spain’s Alexia Putellas securing the women’s award for a third time

/football/2026/oct/30/ballon-dor-betting.headline: Ballon d’Or ceremony returns to England in nod to ‘revolutionary’ Stanley Matthews
/football/2026/oct/30/ballon-dor-betting.excerpt: When football’s dignitaries assemble on Monday at the London Palladium for the Ballon d’Or ceremony it will be a far cry from the first awards 70 years ago. That was held in the slightly less glamorous surroundings of Blackpool town hall, where Stanley Matthews was presented with the prize by Gabriel Hanot, the visionary editor of L’Équipe who came up with the idea of crowning the world’s best player every year. A specially commissioned china plate was also handed over by the town’s mayor before the 41-year-old Matthews, who was famously teetotal, gave a short speech. “He might have had a double carrot juice that day,” says his son, Stanley Matthews Jr, who will attend this year’s awards with his sister, Jean, and her two daughters. “There was no ceremony. ‘Here’s your Ballon d’Or, well done’, sort of thing. But obviously it’s grown over the years, and now it’s a huge event. We’re very excited.” The switch of venue to England from its usual home in Paris is a mark of respect to the man who became the first active player to receive a knighthood in 1965, a few months before retiring at the age of 50. It also provides an opportunity to recall an astonishing career that began with his local side Stoke in 1932 and made the “Wizard of Dribble” the most famous player on the planet. “He was so far ahead of his time,” says Matthews Jr, a former winner of junior Wimbledon who had a successful tennis career.
/football/2026/oct/30/ballon-dor-betting.trail: Matthews’ family ‘very excited’ as London Palladium hosts event 70 years after first award at Blackpool town hall

/football/2026/oct/30/ballon-dor-betting.headline: Harry Kane says wait to learn if he has won Ballon d’Or is stressful for family
/football/2026/oct/30/ballon-dor-betting.excerpt: Harry Kane would love to know now whether he has won the Ballon d’Or because the uncertainty and constant questions are driving his family to distraction. But the Bayern Munich and England striker accepts the suspense before the big reveal at the London Palladium on Monday night is part of the show. Kane is the odds-on favourite to win the prestigious individual honour after a prolific run of form. The 33-year-old scored 61 goals for Bayern last season and 12 for England. This time out, he has 10 for Bayern and six for England. He scored from the penalty spot in Wednesday’s 2-2 Champions League draw against Arsenal at the Allianz Arena, although his standout moment was the inch-perfect through ball that set up Alphonso Davies to make it 1-1. Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal is the second-favourite for the Ballon d’Or and Kylian Mbappé of Real Madrid is next in the betting. “I think my wife would prefer to know and my family … it’s very stressful for everyone,” Kane said. “I can see why they don’t tell people. They want everyone to go, all the big names, and there will be more people watching it if they don’t know so I can understand why. “From my point of view, I’d love to know to just kind of see and not have to wait throughout the whole night. But it is their decision, I can’t control that. We’ll have to just enjoy it and try not to stress out too much. “I try not to think about it. Obviously it is hard not to.

Hillingdon’s pet dogs produce about 174 tonnes of faeces each year, which, until now, has been generally bagged up by their owners and deposited in dog-waste bins. The Conservative-run council believes it will save £100,000 in waste collection costs by removing the bins. It hopes dog owners will use general litter bins instead, but O’Neill and many other people are unconvinced. “Everybody’s going to have a Christmas tree of dog-shit baubles in their front garden because there’ll be nowhere else to put the bags of it,” O’Neill said. “I got one of those AI generators to make me a Christmas tree with dog-shit bags in different colours, to show what’s going to happen.” Sital Punja who walks Marley, her springer-poodle, every day in Ruislip woods, said the “preposterousness” of the bin removals have dominated chat between dog walkers. “People are really unhappy about it, it’s going to be dumped everywhere,” said Punja, who is an opposition Labour councillor. “The dog bins in the woods are already overflowing and there aren’t enough general bins. The dog bins have lids so the smell stays inside.

/uk-news/2026/oct/30/men-accused-of-sexu.headline: More prisoners recalled to jail than released in England and Wales
/uk-news/2026/oct/30/men-accused-of-sexu.excerpt: More people were recalled to jails in England and Wales in the first half of this year than were released, despite government efforts to reduce the prison population, according to figures released on Thursday. Ministry of Justice (MoJ) data shows that 12,338 people were recalled to custody between the beginning of April and the end of June, while 12,278 people were released. It continues a trend set between January and March, when 13,193 people were returned to prison and 12,977 released. A total of 52,716 prisoners were put back behind bars in the year to June after breaching the terms of their licence – 27% up on the previous 12-month total. The high recall rate is a key contributor to the prison capacity crisis and helped to prompt early release schemes earlier this month. The MoJ figures also show 79,274 inmates were freed early from prison between September 2024 and June 2026 under emergency measures brought in by the government to try to tackle the overcrowding crisis. The move, known as the SDS40 early release scheme, cut the proportion of sentences some prisoners must serve in England and Wales from 50% to 40%. It is one of several policy changes that are likely to have contributed to the rise in recalls, the MoJ said. The emergency measures were replaced with a permanent scheme for early releases from 1 October under the Sentencing Act 2026.

/uk-news/2026/oct/30/men-accused-of-sexu.excerpt: Russell Brand’s wife has told a court that they previously split up over his promiscuity but that he was a “wonderful father” and an “amazingly attentive husband”. Giving evidence at her husband’s rape trial, Laura Brand, 39, said they fell in love after meeting in 2006 but that the comedian found monogamy difficult. “I wasn’t interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people,” she said. Brand, 51, is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges. Giving evidence at Southwark crown court on Wednesday, Laura told the court she met Brand at the Edinburgh festival in 2006 after his show Shame, which was “very, very, very funny”, “extremely entertaining” and sexually explicit. She said they met in the foyer of the Assembly Rooms, where Brand complimented her friend, who had a boyfriend. Laura recalled: “And he said to me: ‘But tell me you don’t have a boyfriend,’ and I said: ‘No, I don’t.’” Laura recalled that Brand contacted her the next day and they had oral sex. Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, asked: “Did he want to have penetrative sex?” to which Laura replied: “I didn’t want to, but I don’t remember it even being a topic. I didn’t intend to and I don’t remember him asking.” They began dating in September 2006 and Brand “absolutely” respected her wishes sexually, Laura said.

/uk-news/2026/oct/30/men-accused-of-sexu.headline: Neighbour of new Montenegro embassy in London sues council over impact on mental health
/uk-news/2026/oct/30/men-accused-of-sexu.excerpt: It is not a classic neighbour-from-hell dispute, what with the protagonist inviting everyone over for evening drinks and canapés. But the sudden conversion of a five-bedroom family home in Pimlico, central London, into the embassy of Montenegro has triggered a neighbourhood row that has gone all the way to the desk of a high court judge. The first stirrings of trouble came when one resident argued in a submission to the council this spring that the new embassy’s “flagpole and rather tacky-looking flag stick out like a sore thumb” among Cambridge Street’s Grade II-listed homes. A second person, who described Montenegro’s red flag with gold border as “gaudy”, suggested the embassy was “out of keeping with the quietly dignified” whitewash late-Regency frontages designed by Thomas Cubitt. Some of those critics, frustrated by the lack of planning application before the installation of the embassy flagpole and plaque, were somewhat placated when drinks were put on by the chargé d’affaires of the west Balkans state. “Perhaps it would have been diplomatic to have done that at the start,” one resident commented drily. But the party did not convince everyone, and an involuntary nextdoor neighbour to the embassy has now taken matters to the courts. Diana Simpson, 35, an Ivy league graduate who lives with her parents on Cambridge Street, is suing Westminster city council.

Joanne Young said that on one occasion she managed to remove her blindfold and was shocked to glimpse a stranger in her bedroom whom her then husband, Philip Young, had allegedly arranged to have sex with her. On another occasion she came around feeling “terrified”, with her husband asking her: “Wouldn’t you like it if somebody else was here?” Philip Young, 50, “advertised” Joanne Young on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court has heard. He has pleaded guilty to multiple charges of abuse, but four men who allegedly sexually assaulted Joanne Young, having been invited into the couple’s home by Philip Young, are on trial. Recorded video interviews of Joanne Young, 49, telling her story to the police were watched by the jury on Wednesday. Joanne Young said she and her husband had been married for 20 years and had three children. She said they were a straight, monogamous couple. “It was always just the two of us,” she said. On one occasion early on in their marriage, he “joked” about watching her when she was having sex with someone else but she “laughed it off”. She said: “That was never part of our relationship and was never going to be.” He liked to restrain and blindfold her during sex.

/world/2026/oct/31/us-cancels-g20-family.headline: Albanese looks for reset on world stage as ‘spot fires burn’ domestically and likely interest rate hike looms
/world/2026/oct/31/us-cancels-g20-family.excerpt: As “summit season” begins, reaffirming ties with fellow leaders on the world stage could be a circuit breaker for Anthony Albanese amid domestic and economic woes, analysts have said. But a likely interest rate hike, triggered by higher-than-expected inflation, while the prime minister is overseas will make his job – and the treasurer’s – even harder. Albanese is attending the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda from Saturday. He will hold talks with King Charles III and allies including the UK and Canadian prime ministers, Andy Burnham and Mark Carney, at the biennial meeting. The discussions will constitute a well-needed reset after controversies over grant funding and pressures on inflation, according to Dr Zareh Ghazarian, an associate professor of politics at Monash University. “It is a strategically important time for him,” Ghazarian said. “He’s got a lot of spot fires burning domestically but this is going to be an opportunity for him to present himself to be much more on the front foot. “There’s a lot of pressure, so this trip could just be a moment to reset the political debate for people … this is a critical moment to present himself as a world leader amongst other world leaders.” Albanese will be away when the Reserve Bank hands down its next interest rate decision on Tuesday, with markets tipping a rise to 4.85%.
